# CrypTool

A free cryptography teaching application developed by German universities, built to make
cryptographic mechanisms **visible** rather than merely available. Version **1** carries labs 01–06 of
[[cybersecurity-engineering-laboratories]] — the entire cryptography half of the course.

## What it provides

| Menu area | Used for |
|---|---|
| Encrypt/Decrypt → Symmetric (Classic) | Caesar, substitution, Playfair, Vigenère, Hill, ADFGVX, homophonic |
| Encrypt/Decrypt → Symmetric (Modern) | DES, 3DES, AES, RC4 |
| Analysis → Tools for analysis | entropy, ASCII frequency histograms, autocorrelation, periodicity, n-grams, floating frequency |
| Analysis → Symmetric (Classic) → Ciphertext-only | automatic cipher-breaking |
| Analysis → Asymmetric | prime generation, RSA factorisation, lattice attacks on RSA |
| Indiv. Procedures → RSA Cryptosystem | keygen, factorisation of a supplied modulus |
| Demonstrations | Diffie–Hellman, hash collisions, digital signature workflow |

The analysis menu is why the tool is worth a page: it turns [[cryptanalysis-by-measurement]] from an
idea into a two-click experiment. Encrypt a text, measure its entropy, plot its histogram, compare
against the plaintext — the comparison *is* the lesson, and it happens in seconds.

## What it demonstrates well

- **Entropy and histograms side by side** across six languages and every classical cipher, producing
  the ranking on [[cryptanalysis-by-measurement]].
- **Autocorrelation recovering a key length** for polyalphabetic ciphers — a parameter recovered by
  measurement, not by guessing.
- **A hash collision breaking a signature**, which is the clearest possible statement of why
  collision resistance is the load-bearing hash property. See [[digital-signatures]].
- **The Diffie–Hellman exchange as a walkthrough**, with each participant's values shown at each step.

## Its limits, as the labs found them

- **Only CBC and ECB** among block cipher modes. The lab reached OFB and CFB through an online
  encryption service instead — see [[block-cipher-modes]]. That is a real gap in a tool being used to
  teach modes of operation, and pushing key material through a third-party web page to fill it is a
  practice hazard whatever the pedagogy.
- **Stability.** The lab-02 report records the application crashing when asked for a histogram after
  homophonic encryption.
- **Automatic breaking is not reliable on modern ciphers**, which is the correct result: the lab-05
  brute-force exercises against AES recovered a direction rather than a key, and the report says so.
- **CrypTool 1 is the oldest of the family** (CrypTool 2, JCrypTool and CrypTool-Online all exist).
  **TODO:** why version 1 was used is not recorded in the repository. Do not infer a preference —
  `confidence: low` on the motivation, `confidence: high` on the fact.

## Why a teaching tool earns a wiki page

Because the alternative shapes the learning. Writing the same experiments against OpenSSL or a Python
library gives real artefacts and no visualisation; CrypTool gives visualisation and leaves nothing
reviewable behind — every result is a screenshot in a report rather than a script someone could re-run.
That trade shows up directly in this repository: the crypto labs are PDFs of observations, while the
one thing that *is* reproducible is a 50-line Python fixture generator. See
[[generate-fixtures-not-commit]] and, for the contrast, [[openssl]].
